newsitem.title: USA: SOCCER-MLS OFFICIALS TERM INAUGURAL SEASON A SUCCESS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MLS OFFICIALS TERM INAUGURAL SEASON A SUCCESS.

text.p: Major League Soccer officials, gathered here for the league's first championship match on Sunday, hailed their inaugural season as a success and promised to make more gains next season.

MLS commissioner Doug Logan, speaking on the eve of MLS Cup '96 pitting D.C. United against the Los Angeles Galaxy, cited several high water marks for the league, including higher than anticipated attendance and sponsorship deals.
"We've earned some spurs and achieved some credible goals," Logan said. "But we're not going to sit on any laurels. We know we have a long way to go."
"In the coming season, we are going to work longer and harder."

More than 40,000 tickets have been sold for the final at nearby Foxboro, with officials hoping for a crowd of 50,000 to see the title tilt between Eastern Conference champion D.C. United and the Western winners Galaxy.
Both teams have fairly wide open attacks.
El Salvadoran striker Raul Diaz Arce, Bolivian midfielder playmaker Marco Etcheverry and U.S. national team member John Harkes lead United.

The Galaxy, directed by former U.S. national team coach Lothar Osiander, rely upon Mexican international goalkeeper, El Salvadoran midfielder Mauricio Cienfuegos and Ecuadoran forward Eduardo Hurtado.

Among the accomplishments touted by Logan was a high quality of play, higher attendance than originally predicted, losses about $7 million less than the anticipated $25 million and solid sponsor support.

Pepsi-Cola was announced as the league's ninth sponsor Friday as the exclusive soft drink, which increased MLS sponsorship and advertising sales to $70 million. The $10 million, three-year deal will include sponsorship of the U.S. national team and youth soccer as well.
"We did what we said we were going to do," Logan said at a news conference Friday. "We said we were going to have aggressive, high quality style and we did.
"We started out with a sensible business plan and we stuck with it."
Harkes agreed. "What we've done in the past six months is incredible," he said. "The level of play is intense. I have no doubt this league will go far and do very well."
MLS exceeded admittedly modest attendance projections of between 10,000-12,000 a a game, attracting an average of 17,416 during the regular season, and an average of 16,163 in the playoffs.
A sizeable part of the audience was Hispanic.
"We opened our arms to new audiences," Logan said. "Over 40 percent of our audiences nationally are ethnics, first or second generation Americans, and mostly Latinos.

"We have appealed to the best of the American principles. We exemplify tough competition. We exemplify fair play. We exemplify access to all. We exemplify inclusion for all races, gender and economic classes."
Logan said next season's goals include a 15 percent increase in attendance.
The league also wants to expand by two teams to 12 in 1999. Charlotte and Houston are considered to be the top contenders, although Chicago would be given a franchise if a stadium was available.
